This is an area of car design I find particularly interesting. After WWI many European countries created programs to develop and provide small light cars to disabled veterans and this produced an interesting period of cladogenesis in vehicle engineering and design. A really exuberant phase of experimentation in the history of the car. At the time there was a class of car we no longer see today called 'cyclecars' or 'velocars' that filled a gap between early motorcycles and full-size cars. They were small forms of cars typified by their use of bicycle-style wheels and often featuring wooden body construction. One of the most successful of these was the Briggs & Stratton Flyer or Red Bug which may have been the first mainstream enthusiast's automobile and one of the first practical electric cars. It may have been one of the inspirations for the design of the Apollo Lunar Rover. At the time the full-size car was still a high luxury product relying on the kind of series production typical of today's supercars. Governments wanted to improve the lives of veterans through mobility, providing vehicles that could be operated by people missing one or more limbs and were suited to the modest distances of the village or city. And so a this great assortment of strange and clever little cars appeared to meet this demand. By WWII the cyclecar largely disappeared and automobile fabrication became dominated by the pressed steel welded unibody construction common today. But some of these veterans programs persisted after the war and combined with increasing concerns about the safety of using full-size cars in Europe's dense cities. So a new class of 'microcar' developed based on more modern engines and fabrication. This produced such well known and still much-loved microcars as the BMW Isetta and the Messerschmitt. The superhighway and the suburbs largely killed-off the microcar, though experimentation continued to persist in Europe. It was briefly revived with the Oil Crisis of the 70s and new interest in pedal-powered velocars and electric powered vehicles.

The potential of today's new higher performance battery and electric motor technology has again revived interest in microvehicles of all sorts--from hoverboards to novel cars. We're entering a new phase of cladogenesis in car design as the virtues of electric power trains are finally being realized, allowing for a range of unusual vehicles with previously impossible forms like the wheelchair car in this video. We're going to soon see an explosion in unusual vehicles in all sizes as increasingly modular electric drive systems and automated driving control systems empower increasing experimentation by amateurs and pros alike. Already one can buy open source kits for DIY EV development. We may soon see (perhaps more likely in Asia first) car dealerships rather like custom PC shops building whole cars on demand from stock parts. Having cars assembled at the dealership may soon be the norm.

One of my favorite microcars is the 1950s Czechoslovakian Velorex Oskar. The Velorex company is well known as a maker of side-cars for motorcycles but for some time they also produced small cars. The cool thing about the Oskar is that, being in a relatively poor country, they needed to re-think how a car was made. The gigantic machines used for pressed steel bodies were long unattainable. But as car engineers know, space frames are the smart way to go when you want high performance, high durability, and low weight. That's why most race cars and extreme off-road vehicles use these. So Velorex designed the Oskar with a welded tube space frame chassis. But a practical car can't have an open chassis like this. It needs to be enclosed to shelter people from wind and rain. They didn't have a very high-tech way to do that so they covered the car in a removable skin of fabric and faux leather. It's a leather-covered car. And this worked surprisingly well in even the rough winters of the region--though it probably wasn't that comfortable. Why this never became the standard car among developing world countries I find hard to understand. Any industry capable of bicycles and motorcycles could make cars like the Oskar.

Today there is a well established industry across the US producing chassis for street legal motor trikes using car engines. It's a strange but popular custom vehicle among motorcycle enthusiasts and apparently in many states keeping under four wheels lets them skirt a lot of obstructive regulations. These companies are sort-of like custom PC shops. The chassis are more-or-less public domain designs and they outfit them with off-the-shelf parts to make a working vehicle. I think these could easily produce a chassis like that of the Oskar'a and combine it with a modular electric power train and more modern materials, like the tension roof materials like teflon-impregnated fiberglass cloth (as used in roofs like that of the Denver Airport), as a body skin. This would allow for hundreds of new little car companies locally producing their own EVs, experimenting with new designs, and create a new industry of module EV components. You could easily build your own car at home just as you can build a PC.
